title: Why Everyday Investors Sell Winners Early and Hold Losers
alt_title_1: Terrance Odean's 10,000-Account Study on the Disposition Effect
alt_title_2: Stop Cutting Your Flowers to Water Financial Weeds
description_hook: Coined by Hersh Shefrin and Meir Statman in 1985 and tested across 10,000 brokerage accounts by Terrance Odean in 1998, the Disposition Effect shows how selling winners early and holding losers costs everyday investors 3.4% in subsequent annual returns.

scenes.headline: Why Amateur Traders Cash Winners and Hug Losers
scenes.stat_label: PRIDE CHASES QUICK GAINS; REGRET HIDES LOSSES
bullets: 15% gain triggers an urge to lock in pride
scenes.narration: Why do everyday investors cash out winning stocks for tiny gains while clinging to sinking losers for years? Pride and regret.

scenes.headline: Shefrin, Statman & Odean's Brokerage Proof
scenes.stat_label: SOLD WINNERS BEAT HELD LOSERS OVER NEXT 12 MONTHS
bullets: Shefrin & Statman (1985) named the Disposition Effect
Odean (1998) verified it across 10,000 real accounts
scenes.narration: Hersh Shefrin and Meir Statman named this the Disposition Effect in 1985. In 1998, Terrance Odean analyzed ten thousand brokerage accounts and found the sold winners went on to beat held losers by three-point-four percent.
scenes.source: Shefrin & Statman, J. Finance (1985); Terrance Odean, J. Finance (1998)

scenes.headline: Cutting Your Flowers to Water Your Weeds
scenes.left_body: Anchors to purchase price -> sells compounders, bags dead weight
scenes.right_body: Automated broad index funds + fresh-cash thesis checks
scenes.narration: Selling a winner locks in quick pride, while holding a loser delays admitting a mistake, leaving you trimming flowers to water your weeds.

scenes.headline: Automate Broad Indexes or Run the Fresh-Cash Test
scenes.stat_label: UNINTERRUPTED WINNERS DRIVE LONG-TAIL PORTFOLIO RETURNS
scenes.stat_subtext: Index funds auto-let winners grow • Zero break-even anchoring
scenes.narration: Erase ego from your portfolio: automate low-cost broad index funds, or ask whether you would buy a losing stock today with fresh cash.

scenes.headline: The Market Does Not Know Your Entry Price
scenes.stat_label: NEVER ANCHOR TO WHAT YOU PAID YESTERDAY
bullets: Break-even is a psychological mirage, not a strategy
Let automated broad indexes ride multi-decade winners
scenes.narration: Judge every holding by tomorrow's math instead of yesterday's purchase price, and let true compounders run.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule based on Shefrin & Statman (1985) and Odean (1998)
